## Example 3.2 · Checking differences {#ss3-example-3-2 .ap-lesson}

Consider the sequence $\displaystyle\frac12,\frac16,-\frac16,\ldots$

<div class="ap-subparts"><p><span class="ap-part-label">a)</span> Show that this sequence is arithmetic.</p><p><span class="ap-part-label">b)</span> Hence, state the common difference of this arithmetic sequence.</p><p><span class="ap-part-label">c)</span> Find the next term of this sequence.</p></div>

<p class="small-note">Checking two differences establishes that the three displayed terms are in arithmetic progression.</p>

<p class="booklet-cue">Booklet p. 11 · Example 3.2</p>

::: notes

Preserve the booklet question, while explicitly observing its limitation: a finite prefix alone cannot prove an unspecified infinite continuation. The intended continuation uses a constant difference. For the displayed terms, 1/6−1/2=−1/3 and −1/6−1/6=−1/3. Thus d=−1/3 and the intended next term is −1/2.
For a genuine all-terms proof, if needed write the intended rule a_n=1/2−(n−1)/3, then subtract a_(n−1)=1/2−(n−2)/3 to obtain −1/3 for every n≥2. Do not repeat the old slides' claim that checking only T3−T2=T2−T1 proves the whole infinite sequence.

:::
